title: Refine Drugs, Don't Complete Them: Uniform-Source Discrete Flows for Fragment-Based Drug Discovery
one_liner: Generate new drugs by refining all parts of a molecule in parallel, instead of building it word by word.
lead: Drug discovery starts with fragments—small pieces of molecules known to bind to disease targets. Chemists want to grow these fragments into full drugs while keeping desired properties like potency and safety. Current models work like writing: they predict one token (chemical piece) at a time, deciding what comes next. InVirtuoGen instead flips this: it starts with a completely scrambled molecule and refines all parts at once, like unblurring a photo. This parallel refinement is faster because all atoms refine in one pass instead of requiring one pass per atom, and it keeps better track of chemistry constraints because later refinement steps can fix early mistakes, preventing errors from cascading.

problem.h2: Why token-by-token drug generation gets stuck
paras: In drug discovery, a chemist starts with a molecular fragment—a small piece known to bind a disease target. The goal is to grow it into a full drug by adding atoms and bonds while keeping potency (it still binds), safety (it is not toxic), and synthetic feasibility (a lab can actually make it). Current generative models treat this like language: they predict one chemical symbol at a time. After predicting the first symbol, they predict the second conditioned on the first, then the third, and so on. This sequential approach has two problems. First, early mistakes cascade—a wrong first symbol steers the entire generation down a bad path. Second, the model must make a decision about whether to continue for every single position in the final molecule, so a 50-token drug requires 50 decision steps, and each decision point is a chance to fail.

A beginner might try: just use a standard language model or autoregressive model (a model that predicts one token at a time). But chemists have learned that constraints on bond valence, aromaticity, and ring closure are fragile under sequential prediction. The model often produces chemically invalid molecules—structures with too many bonds on an atom or impossible ring patterns. It wastes generation steps on fixing mistakes instead of exploring promising regions of chemical space.

callout.html: InVirtuoGen treats drug generation as refinement—start with noise, refine all atoms and bonds in parallel—rather than sequential completion.

paras: InVirtuoGen changes the generation direction from token-by-token completion to full-molecule refinement. Instead of predicting what comes next, the model predicts the entire molecule in parallel refinement steps. This decouples the number of sampling steps (how many times we refine) from the sequence length (how many atoms the drug has). The model learns to map a uniform random source (pure noise, no structure) to the data distribution (valid drugs with known properties). By refinement rather than completion, every position can change at every step, correcting early errors and exploring chemistry space more flexibly.
object.object: Generation direction: refinement instead of completion

hidden.name: Validity and chemical coherence during refinement steps
paras: Refinement trajectory measures how smoothly the model transforms noise into a valid, drug-like molecule. At each denoising step, atoms and bonds shift, and the model must maintain chemical validity (no atom with too many bonds, no broken rings) while gradually assembling a structure that matches the training distribution (real drugs). This is not just counting valid molecules at the end—it is tracking whether every intermediate step stays chemically sound.

InVirtuoGen estimates trajectory coherence by computing which positions change at each step, whether those changes respect chemistry constraints, and whether the resulting molecule grows closer to a valid drug structure. The paper uses this implicitly by training the model to predict all positions at every denoising step, forcing the model to learn smooth refinement paths. Molecules that maintain validity throughout refinement can continue learning; trajectories that collapse into invalid structures are down-weighted in the loss. This is why parallel refinement works: the model learns to avoid local chemical dead-ends by correcting all atoms together.

heat.caption: Darker means more chemistry coherence. Highlighted cells show refinement steps that maintain validity.

reads.html: Refinement trajectory is like unblurring a photo. At first, every atom is equally fuzzy (uniform noise). Each step clarifies some atoms and bonds, refining the entire picture. If any step creates a chemically invalid structure (like an atom with 5 bonds), the model learns to backtrack. Valid trajectories are rewarded; broken ones are penalized.

The loss accounts for predictions on all sequence positions at every denoising step, not just the final step. This forces the model to learn valid refinement paths. By contrast, masked models only check validity at the end. InVirtuoGen's loss is computed at every denoising step and every position in the molecule, summing the log probabilities. This means even small mistakes in intermediate refinement steps are penalized, teaching the model smooth valid paths.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: parallel refinement avoids early mistakes
paras: Sequential models fail because the first prediction commits the model to a path. If token 1 is wrong, tokens 2 through N must compensate or fail. Refinement flips this: all tokens start equally uncertain (uniform noise), and every step improves all of them together. Early errors do not cascade because later steps can correct them. If the model predicts the wrong atom at position 5 in step 1, step 2 can fix it when the model sees the evolving context of the whole molecule.

The second advantage is computational: sequential generation needs one forward pass per token, so a 50-token drug requires 50 passes. Refinement can use the same number of denoising steps regardless of length—a 30-token fragment and a 50-token drug both use 10 steps. This is because refinement is not deciding how many steps to take; it is deciding how much noise to remove at each step. The model learns to prioritize: in early steps, rough shapes (where is the core ring structure); in late steps, fine details (which substituent side chain). This focus prevents the model from wasting computation on micro-decisions. The training loss also reflects this: by computing the loss at every position and every denoising step, the model learns to refine valid molecules smoothly, because invalid intermediate structures produce high loss across many positions and steps.

Denoising step 1: refine all atoms in parallel, rough shapes emerge
Denoising steps 2-N: incrementally clarify all bonds and side chains

Newly generated drug candidate: valid, potent, safe, synthesizable

math.words: Total loss sums predictions at all positions during all denoising steps, favoring molecules with smooth valid refinement paths
math.equation: L = sum_t sum_i log p(x_i^t | x_noised^t) where x_i^t is atom i at denoising step t
symbols: Predicted atom type at position i, denoising step t
Partially denoised molecule up to step t
Denoising step (1, 2, ..., T; T is final step)
Position in the molecule (atom index, 1 to N)
Probability the model assigns to that prediction
Log likelihood (higher is better, used to measure prediction confidence)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have a 5-token drug and 3 denoising steps (T=3).
Step 1 (rough): model predicts [C, C, X, X, X] where X means 'uncertain'. Loss_1 = log(0.8) + log(0.8) + log(0.1) + log(0.1) + log(0.1) ≈ 1.6 + 1.6 - 2.3 - 2.3 - 2.3 = -3.8.
Step 3 (final): model predicts [C, C, O, N, H]. Loss_3 = log(0.95) + log(0.95) + log(0.95) + log(0.85) + log(0.9) ≈ -0.26.

Total loss = -3.8 - 0.57 - 0.26 = -4.63. Smooth refinement (improving predictions at each step) yields less total loss than chaotic or invalid intermediate states, so the model learns valid trajectories.

math.note: By summing loss over all steps and all positions, the model is penalized for invalid intermediate molecules, not just wrong final answers. This teaches refinement coherence.

charts.title: Sequential token-by-token models
charts.note: Sequential generation limits exploration; early errors and constraint violations reduce both the range of structures found and potency.

charts.title: InVirtuoGen with parallel refinement
charts.note: Parallel refinement explores more of chemistry space; smooth trajectories avoid invalid structures; genetic plus property-guided optimization tune multi-objective tradeoffs.

items.html: If the fragment (the starting chemical piece) is small or weakly anchored in the training data, refinement might drift away from it. The model may generate drugs that ignore the fragment's binding mode, wasting effort. Constraining fragment tokens is necessary but adds computational overhead.

If all top candidates converge to a narrow region of chemistry space (e.g., all have the same core ring), breeding no longer explores new structures. Diversity is lost. The algorithm needs mechanisms to preserve fitness variation or restart exploration.

Finetuning for a specific property (e.g., binding score) without brakes can cause the model to memorize a single high-scoring molecule instead of learning a distribution of good drugs. The finetuned model then fails on related but different targets.

When fragment anchoring is enforced, genetic diversity is maintained, and property-guided optimization uses careful braking (preventing the model from chasing a single solution too hard), InVirtuoGen generates new multi-objective-balanced drugs that pass chemistry validity and docking checks, improving on all benchmarks.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A minimal demo starts with one fragment (e.g., an indole known to bind a kinase) and runs InVirtuoGen to generate 100 drug candidates optimizing 3 goals: binding strength, low toxicity, and synthesis feasibility. It measures 5 metrics: coverage (percentage of generated drugs unseen in training), validity (percentage with correct chemistry), potency (average docking score, how well each drug binds), and multi-objective coverage (fraction of the Pareto frontier—candidates where no other candidate beats them at all three goals at once). A second demo shows lead optimization starting from a weak hit (a molecule that binds but is toxic) and breeding toward a balanced drug. Code should be under 300 lines: initialize fragment, run denoising loop with validity checking, rank by genetic fitness, apply property-guided finetuning, and compute metrics.
demo.metric_eq: Pareto_coverage = count(candidates_on_frontier) / total_candidates; Validity = count(chemically_valid) / count(generated)
demo.closing: A successful demo makes clear: parallel refinement finds more unseen drug structures than sequential models, maintains chemistry validity throughout, and multi-objective optimization produces drugs excelling at all three goals—potent and safe and synthesizable at once.
